issues.legal_issue: State acquisition powers cannot be used as a device to transfer acquired land to a private developer for private benefit.
material_facts: The land was initially notified for development of public urban sectors.
The developer entered the matter after the acquisition notification, did not own the land before that notification, and sought licences for colonisation of land under acquisition.
The developer paid landowners to enter into agreements while they faced the threat of losing their land through acquisition.
After the award, state authorities released acquired land and granted licences to the developer, followed by transfers of title to it.
The record supported the finding that the purported landowner applications concealed the developer’s role and that state action enabled the developer to obtain the land.
issues.conclusion: The release of acquired land and the resulting transfer to the developer were an abuse and colourable exercise of public power, contrary to the public purpose and the constitutional guarantees of equality, life and property. The release orders and consequential transactions in favour of the developer could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Compulsory acquisition must serve a compelling public purpose and cannot be used to enable a private entity to obtain title or profit from the land. Public power is held in trust, must be exercised objectively and transparently, and cannot be used for a purpose different from that for which it was conferred. The Court applied Articles 14, 21 and 300-A of the Constitution and Section 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894. It relied on the public trust doctrine in Reliance Natural Resources Ltd. v. Reliance Industries Ltd., Centre for Public Interest Litigation v. Union of India, Special Reference No. 1 of 2012 and Manohar Lal Sharma v. Principal Secretary; on colourable exercise and fraud on power in State of Punjab v. Gurdial Singh and Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority v. Devendra Kumar; and on Royal Orchid Hotels v. G. Jayarama Reddy for the vitiating effect of fraud in land acquisition-related action.

rule.if: land_acquisition_challenge and (developer_entered_after_acquisition_notice and developer_lacked_prior_land_title) and state_released_acquired_land_to_developer and (release_defeated_notified_public_purpose or state_action_enabled_private_title_transfer)

predicates.land_acquisition_challenge: A party challenged state action involving acquisition of land and its subsequent release or transfer.
predicates.developer_entered_after_acquisition_noti: A private developer entered the transaction after the state had notified the land for acquisition.
predicates.developer_lacked_prior_land_title: The developer did not own the land before the acquisition process began.
predicates.state_released_acquired_land_to_develope: State authorities released land under acquisition to the developer.
predicates.release_defeated_notified_public_purpose: The release prevented or undermined the public purpose for which the land had been acquired.
predicates.state_action_enabled_private_title_trans: State action enabled a private developer to obtain title to land that it could not otherwise have acquired through the acquisition process.

issues.definition: When a land-acquisition challenge shows that the state released acquired land to a developer who entered after the acquisition process and lacked prior title, and that the release undermined the public purpose or enabled a private title transfer, the release is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A later unlawful release of land does not invalidate an acquisition that was initially made for a genuine public purpose.
material_facts: The acquisition had been initiated and completed for a genuine public purpose of developing urban sectors.
The abuse arose from later events, including the release of acquired land to the developer and the associated licences and transfers.
The High Court had quashed the acquisition in its entirety, but the Supreme Court distinguished the valid acquisition from the later unlawful actions.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition notifications and awards were upheld, and the land vested in HUDA. The release orders, licences and transactions in favour of the developer were quashed.
issues.legal_principle: A valid acquisition for a public purpose is distinct from subsequent unlawful action to release the acquired land to a private party. Where the release is mala fide or arbitrary, the acquisition of the released land stands revived. The Court applied the scheme of Sections 4, 6, 16 and 48 of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894, and relied on the principle in Meera Sahni v. Lieutenant Governor of Delhi that an unlawful release does not prevent the acquisition from standing.

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_and_later_relea: A party challenged both a land acquisition and a later release of the acquired land.
predicates.acquisition_had_genuine_public_purpose: The land was initially acquired to fulfil a genuine public purpose.
predicates.later_release_was_abusive: The state later released the acquired land through an arbitrary or mala fide exercise of power.

issues.definition: Where a genuine public-purpose acquisition is followed by an abusive release, the acquisition remains in force while the release is quashed.

issues.legal_issue: A developer who did not own land before acquisition cannot rely on a colonisation policy or obtain a colonisation licence for land that has vested in the state.
material_facts: The developer admitted that it did not own any of the land before the acquisition notification.
The developer effectively made the licence applications, although the applications were presented as those of landowners.
The applications and licences related to land that had been acquired and, according to the record, had vested in the state before the licences were granted.

The applicable policy concerned land owned or purchased by a developer before the acquisition notification, and the governing state law required an owner seeking to develop a colony to apply and required an inquiry into title.
issues.conclusion: The policy did not apply to the developer, and the licences granted for the acquired land were invalid and were quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 2(d), 2(k) and 3 of the Haryana Development and Regulation of Urban Areas Act, 1975, read with Rule 3 of the Haryana Development and Regulation of Urban Areas Rules, 1976, a coloniser must own the land and the licensing authority must inquire into title. The policy relied on by the developer applied only to developers who owned or had purchased the land before the acquisition notification. Rule 17, which restricts transfer of a licence, did not cure the absence of the required ownership or title.

rule.if: colonisation_licence_challenge and licence_sought_for_acquired_land and developer_lacked_required_land_title and licence_granted_for_colonisation

predicates.colonisation_licence_challenge: A party challenged a licence authorising development of a colony on land subject to acquisition.
predicates.licence_sought_for_acquired_land: The licence application concerned land that had been acquired by the state.
predicates.developer_lacked_required_land_title: The developer did not hold the land ownership or title required to apply for the licence.
predicates.licence_granted_for_colonisation: The licensing authority granted permission to develop a colony on the land.

issues.definition: A colonisation licence for acquired land is invalid when the developer applying for it lacks the land title required to obtain that licence.

issues.legal_issue: The receipt of compensation or sale consideration does not estop a landowner from challenging acquisition-related action that is vitiated by abuse of power.
material_facts: Landowners entered agreements to sell or collaborate with the developer while acquisition threatened their land and their bargaining power was limited.
Some landowners received compensation from the state, consideration from the developer, or both.
The challenged release and transfer were found to be without authority of law and the result of colourable or abusive state action.
issues.conclusion: The challenge was not barred by acceptance of compensation or consideration. Under the final directions, payments from the developer were treated as compensation under the award, and landowners were not required to refund them.
issues.legal_principle: Where an acquisition-related order or transaction is vitiated, receipt of compensation or consideration does not create an estoppel against challenging it, particularly where the landowner had little choice in the face of acquisition. The Court relied on Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority v. Devendra Kumar for the absence of estoppel in those circumstances and applied the principle that unlawful action cannot be insulated by a party’s receipt of payment.

predicates.challenge_to_acquisition_related_action: A landowner challenged state or private action connected with the acquisition of the land.
predicates.challenged_action_vitiated_by_abuse: The challenged action was found to be an unlawful or abusive exercise of power.
predicates.landowner_received_compensation_or_sale_: The landowner had received compensation from the state or sale consideration from a private developer.

issues.definition: A landowner’s receipt of compensation or sale consideration does not bar a challenge to acquisition-related action found to be abusive.

issues.legal_issue: Delay in bringing a constitutional challenge is not an automatic bar where the challenged action is alleged to involve fraud or abuse of power.
material_facts: The challenges concerned licences and releases processed over a continuing period.
The land remained undeveloped when the High Court considered the challenge.
The challenged actions were found to involve fraud, abuse of law and an unlawful transfer of acquired land to a private developer.
issues.conclusion: The delay objection did not require dismissal of the challenge; delay is a matter of judicial discretion, not a jurisdictional bar, and belated review of illegal action based on fraud or abuse may be permitted.
issues.legal_principle: A belated petition under Article 226 is not barred for want of jurisdiction merely because it was filed late; delay is a rule of practice governing discretion. A court may exercise its discretion to quash illegal action founded on fraud or abuse of law even when the challenge is belated. The Court relied on Royal Orchid Hotels v. G. Jayarama Reddy concerning fraud in acquisition-related action.

predicates.constitutional_writ_challenge: A party brought a constitutional writ proceeding to challenge state action.
predicates.challenge_is_delayed: The party brought the challenge after a period of delay.
predicates.challenged_action_involves_fraud_or_abus: The challenged action involved fraud or an abuse of public power.

issues.definition: A delayed constitutional challenge may still be reviewed when the challenged action involves fraud or abuse of power.

issues.legal_issue: A purchaser who acquires an interest in disputed land while litigation is pending cannot rely on that purchase to defeat the challenge or preserve the interest against the court’s order.
material_facts: Some third parties claimed to have purchased plots from the developer while litigation over the land was pending.
The Supreme Court found that subsequent transactions or development did not affect the parties’ rights in the litigation.

The Court quashed the third-party rights created by the developer and stated that purchasers could pursue remedies against the developer, whether they knew of the litigation or it had been concealed from them.
issues.conclusion: Purchases made during the litigation did not defeat the challenge or preserve rights in the land against the Court’s order; affected purchasers were left to pursue their remedies against the developer.
issues.legal_principle: The principle of lis pendens applies to transactions entered into during pending litigation. Such transactions do not displace the rights determined in the litigation, though purchasers may pursue private remedies against the transferor. The Court relied on the principle cited from Meera Sahni v. Lieutenant Governor of Delhi concerning subsequent transactions.

predicates.land_rights_litigation_pending: Litigation concerning rights in land was pending before a court.
predicates.third_party_purchase_during_litigation: A third party purchased or acquired an interest in the disputed land while that litigation was pending.

issues.definition: A purchase made while litigation over land is pending does not defeat the challenge to the disputed transactions.

issues.legal_issue: Relief for an unlawful private transfer following a valid acquisition may preserve the acquisition and restore the land to the public authority while compensating affected landowners and addressing third-party claims.
material_facts: The acquisition had been made for a valid public purpose, but the subsequent releases and transfers to the developer were unlawful.
The Supreme Court found that restoring the land to the original owners was not practicable in the circumstances and that the land should instead remain with HUDA for the notified public purpose.
The developer had paid landowners and the state and claimed expenditure on development, while third parties had paid the developer for plots.
The High Court had quashed the entire acquisition and ordered a different restitution arrangement; the Supreme Court modified that relief.
issues.conclusion: The acquisition notifications and awards were upheld, the land vested in HUDA free from encumbrances, and the release orders, licences, sale deeds and third-party rights were quashed. The landowners’ payments from the developer were treated as compensation; the developer could seek verified reimbursement from HUDA without interest after third-party claims were addressed, and third parties could seek refunds from the available amount or allotment of plots on the stated terms. The state was also directed to provide rehabilitation and resettlement benefits and could inquire into the responsible officials’ conduct.
issues.legal_principle: A court may mould relief to remedy unlawful state action without nullifying a valid acquisition, taking account of the public purpose, the impracticability of restoring the land to its former owners, and the need to address affected landowners and purchasers. The public purpose must be preserved, and the unlawful private transfer must not be legitimised. The Court also applied the principle of lis pendens to later transactions and required the state to act consistently with public trust and non-arbitrariness.

predicates.valid_public_purpose_acquisition: The land was acquired for a valid public purpose.
predicates.abusive_private_release: The acquired land was later released or transferred to a private party through an unlawful exercise of power.
predicates.restoration_to_original_owners_impractic: The circumstances made restoration of the land to its original owners impracticable.
predicates.affected_landowners_or_purchasers_requir: Landowners or purchasers were affected by the unlawful release and required remedial directions.

issues.definition: When a valid acquisition is followed by an abusive private release and restoration to the original owners is impracticable, the acquisition is preserved and relief is adjusted for those affected.
